guide.title: Unit 3: Reasoning, sources, and methods of development: review guide
guide.intro: Arguments respond to one another. This unit practices tracing a line of reasoning, spotting flawed reasoning, introducing and citing sources fairly, judging whether evidence is sufficient, and developing ideas through cause and effect or narrative.

sections.title: Lines of reasoning, sound and flawed
body: A line of reasoning is the sequence of claims and evidence that leads to a conclusion. Trace it by asking what each paragraph claims and how it connects to the thesis.

Common flaws include assuming that because one event followed another it was caused by it, generalizing from too few cases, presenting only two options when more exist, and attacking a person instead of an argument.
points: One vivid example can't prove a broad trend.
Look for alternative explanations a writer ignores.

sections.title: Introducing, citing, and using sufficient evidence
body: When you use a source, attribute it (who said it and why they are credible), integrate it smoothly, and cite it so readers can find it. Paraphrases and summaries need attribution too.
Evidence is sufficient when it covers the claim's scope: a claim about most students needs more than one student's story.
points: Match the strength of a claim to the strength of the evidence.
Use sources in conversation: agree, extend, or push back.

sections.title: Cause-effect and narrative development
body: Cause-effect development traces how one thing leads to another; it is persuasive when each link is supported. Narrative development tells a story that illustrates or grounds a claim.
Writers choose a method to fit their purpose: a narrative can make an abstract problem human, and a causal chain can explain why a solution will work.
points: Each link in a causal chain needs support.
A narrative should serve the claim, not replace it.
Signal causes with words like because, therefore, as a result.

example.prompt: Identify the flaw: “After the town installed new streetlights, the high school's test scores rose. The lights must have helped students study.”
example.solution: It assumes that because the scores rose after the lights were installed, the lights caused the rise. Many other factors could explain it, and no evidence links the lights to studying.

misconceptions: “If B happened after A, A caused B.”
“Paraphrasing means you don't need to credit the source.”
A story illustrates; broad claims need broader evidence.
“Disagreeing with a source weakens your essay.”
Responding to sources shows you understand the conversation.

passages.title: Passage 1: A letter to the editor about the Elm Street pool
text: (1) Five years ago the town closed the Elm Street pool to save money. Since then, the number of children enrolled in the summer swim program at the county pool has fallen by a third. The closure clearly made our children worse swimmers.
(2) Anyone who doubts this should talk to my neighbor, whose son never learned to swim after the pool closed.
(3) The choice before the council is simple: reopen the Elm Street pool or accept a generation that cannot swim.
(4) Some will say the county pool is only a short drive away. But many families in our neighborhood do not own cars, and the bus runs once an hour.

passages.title: Passage 2: What I learned at the food bank
text: (1) The first Saturday I volunteered at the Eastside Food Bank, I was assigned to sort cans. By noon I had filled forty boxes, and I felt proud. Then the manager showed me the line outside: two hundred people, and we had boxes for one hundred and fifty.

(2) The shortage, she explained, had a chain of causes. When the grocery store on Fifth Street closed, the food bank lost its largest donor of fresh produce. With less produce, it bought more canned food, which used up its budget faster. By the end of each month, the shelves were nearly empty.

(3) I went home that day thinking about the line, not the boxes. Charity, I realized, depends on systems as much as on generosity. A town that wants its food bank to work must replace what that one store used to give.

passages.title: Draft 1: A student paragraph that uses sources
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph for an essay about school recess. It may need revision.

(1) Recess helps students focus in class. (2) Recess is good. (3) A pediatric health organization has reported that unstructured breaks improve students' attention when they return to class. (4) My friend Sam says he concentrates better after recess. (5) Therefore, all schools should guarantee at least twenty minutes of recess daily.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student paragraph about a bus route
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph for a letter to the transit authority. It may need revision.

(1) The transit authority cut the Route 9 bus last spring. (2) Many students now walk two miles to school along a road without sidewalks. (3) Walking that far takes time. (4) Restoring Route 9 would make the trip safer and get students to class on time.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the writer's main claim?
choices: The bus to the county pool should run more often than once an hour
The town should reopen the Elm Street pool because its closure hurt children's swimming
Children should take swimming lessons in school during the year
The county pool should be closed so the town can afford to reopen the Elm Street pool
questions.explanation: The letter argues that the closure caused harm and that the council should reopen the pool.
choiceExplanations: The bus schedule is support for the claim; the letter doesn't ask for more buses.
School lessons are never proposed.
The county pool is mentioned as an alternative; the writer never proposes closing it.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, the writer concludes that the closure “clearly made our children worse swimmers.” What is the main weakness in this reasoning?
choices: It relies on a quotation from a swimming expert rather than on the county's enrollment data
It uses too many statistics for readers of a short letter
It ignores the cost of reopening and staffing the Elm Street pool
It assumes that because enrollment fell after the closure, children became worse swimmers
questions.explanation: Lower enrollment after the closure doesn't show that children became worse swimmers, or that the closure was the cause.
choiceExplanations: There is no expert quotation in the paragraph.
The paragraph uses only one statistic, and the flaw is in the reasoning, not the number.
Cost is a fair question, but it isn't the logical flaw in this conclusion.

questions.prompt: The example of the neighbor's son in paragraph 2 is weak support for the writer's claim mainly because
choices: a single case can't show what happened to children in general
it comes from a neighbor rather than from a stranger the writer has not met
it contradicts the statistic in paragraph 1
it describes a boy rather than a girl from the neighborhood
questions.explanation: The claim is about the town's children overall; one child's experience isn't sufficient evidence.
choiceExplanations: Who tells the story matters less than how much it can show.
It's consistent with the statistic; it just can't support the broad claim.
The child's sex is irrelevant to the reasoning.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 3 says the council must either reopen the pool or “accept a generation that cannot swim.” How does paragraph 4 relate to this claim?
choices: It concedes that the Elm Street pool should stay closed because the county pool is just a short drive away
It provides statistics proving that paragraph 3 is correct
It answers an alternative paragraph 3 ignored, which shows that paragraph 3 offered a false choice
It shifts the letter's audience from the council to bus riders
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 addresses the county pool option, a third possibility the either-or framing left out.
choiceExplanations: Paragraph 4 rebuts the objection rather than conceding that the pool should stay closed.
Paragraph 4 contains no statistics; it gives reasons the county pool isn't practical.
The letter still addresses the council.

questions.prompt: Which method of development does the writer mainly use in paragraph 2?
choices: Cause and effect
Definition of a key term
Classification into types
Comparison and contrast
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 traces a chain: the store closes, produce donations drop, the budget runs out, and the shelves empty.
choiceExplanations: The paragraph doesn't define any key term.
It doesn't sort things into types or categories.
No two things are compared point by point.

questions.prompt: The writer begins with the story of sorting cans in order to
choices: explain how food banks are funded by grocery stores and donors
draw readers into the problem through personal experience before explaining causes
show that the writer is a fast, hardworking volunteer who deserves the manager's praise
argue that canned food is better for food banks than fresh produce
questions.explanation: The narrative moves from pride to the shock of the line, leading naturally into the explanation.
choiceExplanations: The story isn't about funding; the causes of the shortage come in paragraph 2.
The writer's speed matters only as a contrast with the size of the need; no praise is mentioned.
The writer doesn't rank canned food above produce.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best expresses the claim the passage builds toward?
choices: “By noon I had filled forty boxes, and I felt proud.”
“Then the manager showed me the line outside: two hundred people, and we had boxes for one hundred and fifty.”
“A town that wants its food bank to work must replace what that one store used to give.”
“With less produce, it bought more canned food, which used up its budget faster.”
questions.explanation: The final sentence states what the narrative and causal chain have been leading to.
choiceExplanations: This is part of the narrative.
This is part of the narrative that shows the need; it doesn't state the claim.
This is a link in the causal chain, not the claim the passage builds toward.

questions.prompt: How do the narrative in paragraph 1 and the causal chain in paragraph 2 work together?
choices: The narrative shows the effect firsthand, and the causal chain explains why it happened
Both present the same information about the shortage in different words
The causal chain disproves the narrative by showing that the food shortage was not real
The narrative introduces a counterargument that the causal chain accepts
questions.explanation: One method makes the shortage vivid; the other makes it understandable, and together they justify the conclusion.
choiceExplanations: They provide different kinds of support: an experience and an explanation.
The causal chain explains why the shortage was real rather than disproving it.
Neither paragraph presents a counterargument.

questions.prompt: Which sentence provides the most credible evidence for the claim in sentence (1)?
choices: Sentence (2)
Sentence (3)
Sentence (5)
Sentence (4)
questions.explanation: Sentence (3) attributes a finding to a relevant health organization.
choiceExplanations: Sentence (2) is an opinion with no support.
Sentence (5) is the conclusion.
One friend's experience is weaker evidence.

questions.prompt: Should the writer keep or delete sentence (2)?
choices: Delete it, because it repeats the idea vaguely and adds no evidence
Delete it, because it contradicts the conclusion in sentence (5)
Keep it, because it is the paragraph's main claim and should come first
Keep it, because it cites a source for the paragraph's claim
questions.explanation: “Recess is good” is vaguer than sentence (1) and offers no support.
choiceExplanations: It doesn't contradict the conclusion; it repeats sentence (1) vaguely.
Sentence (1) is the claim; (2) adds nothing to it.
It cites nothing.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to cite the source in sentence (3) more fully. Which revision is best?
choices: Breaks improve students' attention when they return to class, which is something that teachers and parents already know.
Some experts somewhere have said in reports that breaks are helpful for students' attention in class.
A pediatric organization reported this, according to the internet.
In a 2013 policy statement, the American Academy of Pediatrics reported that unstructured breaks improve students' attention.
questions.explanation: This names the organization and the document and keeps the specific finding. (The American Academy of Pediatrics did publish a 2013 policy statement on recess.)
choiceExplanations: This presents a claim as common knowledge without a source.
This removes the attribution instead of strengthening it.
“The internet” isn't a source readers can check.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Sentence (5) concludes that all schools should guarantee twenty minutes of recess. What would best make this conclusion follow from the evidence?
choices: Delete sentence (3) so the paragraph relies on the student's own experience
Add more stories from friends who say recess helps them concentrate in class
Add evidence linking a specific length of break to attention, or qualify the recommendation
Change “all schools” to “every single school” to make the recommendation sound much stronger
questions.explanation: The evidence shows breaks help but says nothing about twenty minutes or all schools; the writer should support or qualify that leap.
choiceExplanations: Removing the best evidence and relying on anecdote would weaken the paragraph.
More anecdotes still wouldn't support a specific, universal policy.
This makes the claim broader, not better supported.

questions.prompt: Which method of development does the paragraph mainly use?
choices: Description of a place and its features
Definition of a key term
Cause and effect
Comparison and contrast
questions.explanation: It traces the effects of cutting Route 9 and argues that restoring it would reverse them.
choiceExplanations: Description of the road appears, but the paragraph mainly traces causes and effects.
No term is defined.
Nothing is compared point by point.

questions.prompt: Sentence (3) is weak. Which revision best develops the causal link to the writer's claim about getting to class on time?
choices: Some students like walking to school because it gives them time to talk with friends.
The walk takes about forty minutes, and the attendance office reports that first-period tardies have doubled since the cut.
Walking is good exercise for teenagers.
Walking that far takes a very long time, which is bad for students and makes many of their school mornings difficult and stressful.
questions.explanation: It quantifies the effect and links it to tardiness with evidence.
choiceExplanations: This undercuts the argument without addressing time or tardiness.
This argues against the claim instead of supporting it.
This is still vague and gives no evidence of lateness.

questions.prompt: The writer wants to add evidence about safety. Which addition would be most relevant and credible?
choices: The writer's cousin, who walks the road each day, thinks it is dangerous.
Roads without sidewalks can be dangerous for students who walk in many places across the country.
Some roads have sidewalks.
The county's traffic report lists three accidents involving pedestrians on that road last year.
questions.explanation: A specific, attributed finding about this road supports the safety claim.
choiceExplanations: One person's opinion is weaker than recorded data.
This is too general to support a claim about this particular road.
This doesn't address the road in question.

questions.prompt: A transit official might reply that ridership on Route 9 was very low. How could the writer best strengthen the line of reasoning?
choices: Change the topic to bus fares, which affect the many families who ride the bus each day
Ignore the objection to keep the paragraph short
Claim that ridership was actually the highest in the city
Acknowledge low ridership and argue that safety and attendance justify the route anyway
questions.explanation: Addressing a likely objection and explaining why the benefits still matter makes the reasoning harder to dismiss.
choiceExplanations: Changing the subject to fares avoids the ridership issue.
Ignoring an obvious objection leaves the argument vulnerable.
An unsupported claim is flawed reasoning.
